chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-01.title: Meetings of the hands
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-01.body:
The minute hand turns $6^\circ$ per minute and the hour hand $0.5^\circ$ per minute. They first meet again when $6x=0.5x+360$, i.e. $x=\frac{720}{11}$ minutes, and then every $\frac{720}{11}$ minutes. After the $n$-th meeting, $\frac{720n}{11}$ minutes have passed. The seconds hand turns once per minute, so it sits at $\frac{720n}{11}\bmod 1=\frac{5n}{11}\bmod1$ of a full turn.

The hour labels are at multiples of $\frac1{12}$ of a turn, and $\frac{k}{11}$ is closest to the 4:00 label ($\frac13$) exactly for $k=4$ ($\frac4{11}\approx0.364$). So $5n\equiv4\pmod{11}$, i.e. $n\equiv3\pmod{11}$.

Only $n=3$ occurs within the same 12-hour day (the meetings stop after $11$ of them at 12:00 AM). The time is $3\cdot\frac{720}{11}=\frac{2160}{11}\approx196.4$ minutes.

**Answer: 196**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-02.title: Fair sharing
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-02.body:
Let $g,s$ be the total values of gold and silver in the chest and $n$ the number of pirates. Jack's share is $\frac g6+\frac s{10}=\frac{g+s}{n}$, which rearranges to $3s(10-n)=5g(n-6)$. Since $g,s>0$ we need $6<n<10$, so $n\in\{7,8,9\}$.

Jack holds $4$ times as many silver coins as gold coins, and one gold coin is worth $Q$ silver coins, so his gold is worth $Q/4$ times his silver: $Q=4\cdot\frac{g/6}{s/10}=\frac{20g}{3s}$.

- $n=7$: $9s=5g$, so $\frac gs=\frac95$ and $Q=12$.
- $n=8$: $3s=5g$, so $\frac gs=\frac35$ and $Q=4$.
- $n=9$: $s=5g$, so $\frac gs=\frac15$ and $Q=\frac43$.

All satisfy $Q>1$, and the sum is $12+4+\frac43=\frac{52}{3}$.

**Answer: $\frac{52}{3}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-03.title: Complementary counting
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-03.body:
Compute the probability that the 3rd house ends up ranked 4th. Right after it is visited it is at the top (rank 1) or bottom (rank 3) of the 3-house list, each with probability $\frac12$. Each of the 5 later houses is then put above or below it with probability $\frac12$.

- Top: it ends 4th iff exactly $3$ of the $5$ later houses go on top: $\binom53/2^5=\frac{10}{32}$.
- Bottom: it ends 4th iff exactly $1$ later house goes on top: $\binom51/2^5=\frac5{32}$.

So $P(\text{4th})=\frac12\cdot\frac{10}{32}+\frac12\cdot\frac5{32}=\frac{15}{64}$. By the top/bottom symmetry $P(\text{5th})=\frac{15}{64}$ as well.

Hence the answer is $1-\frac{15}{64}-\frac{15}{64}=\frac{17}{32}$.

**Answer: $\frac{17}{32}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-03.title: Direct enumeration
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-03.body:
The first house has no choice, and each of houses $2,\dots,8$ goes to the top or bottom: $2^7=128$ equally likely sequences. Listing all of them, $68$ leave the third house in neither 4th nor 5th place, giving $\frac{68}{128}=\frac{17}{32}$.

**Answer: $\frac{17}{32}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-04.title: Fractional part
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-04.body:
Since $\frac{x+15}4=4+\frac{x-1}4$, the first equation says $\log_3 x=4+\left\{\frac{x-1}4\right\}$ (fractional part), so $4\le\log_3x<5$, i.e. $81\le x<243$. The second condition says $25\le x<125$. So we need solutions with $81\le x<125$.

On each interval $[4k+1,4k+5)$ the right-hand side rises linearly from $4$ to (just below) $5$ with slope $\frac14$. The intervals in our range are $[81,85),[85,89),\dots,[121,125)$: $11$ intervals.

- On $[81,85)$: at $x=81$ both sides equal $4$. Afterwards the right side grows faster (slope $\frac14$) than $\log_3x$ (slope $\frac1{x\ln3}<\frac1{81}$), so there is no other solution.
- On each of the other $10$ intervals: at the left end the right side is $4<\log_3x$, and at the right end it tends to $5>\log_3 x$ (since $\log_3125<5$). So there is a crossing, and since the difference is increasing, exactly one.

Total: $1+10=11$.

**Answer: 11**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-05.title: Residues mod 4
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-05.body:
Every even flavorful number is divisible by $4$. The smallest odd flavorful numbers are $9,25,27$.

*Everything above 30 works.* Multiples of $4$ are sums of distinct powers of $2$ that are at least $4$ (binary expansion), and these powers are flavorful. Then:
- $n\equiv1\pmod4$, $n\ge9$: $n=9+(\text{a multiple of }4)$, with the multiple of $4$ written in distinct powers of two $\ge4$.
- $n\equiv3\pmod4$, $n\ge27$: $n=27+(\text{a multiple of }4)$.
- $n\equiv2\pmod4$, $n\ge34$: $n=9+25+(\text{a multiple of }4)$.
- $n\equiv 0\pmod 4$: binary expansion directly.

Hence every integer $n\ge34$ is representable, and checking the residue classes below $34$ shows $30$ is the largest failure.

*30 does not work.* $30\equiv2\pmod4$. A sum of even flavorful numbers is a multiple of $4$, so the sum needs odd summands, and an even total needs an even number of them, at least two. The two smallest odd flavorful numbers sum to $9+25=34>30$.

**Answer: 30**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-06.title: Coplanarity and the central point
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-06.body:
Put $x_i=A_iP_i$ and let the base rectangle be $A_1A_2A_3A_4$ (so $A_1,A_3$ are opposite corners, as are $A_2,A_4$). Using coordinates with the vertical edges parallel to the $z$-axis, the four points $P_i=(A_i,x_i)$ are coplanar iff $P_1P_2P_3P_4$ is a parallelogram, iff $x_1+x_3=x_2+x_4$.

The three given lengths $3,4,6$ together with the fourth unknown length $x$ must satisfy this with some pairing:
- $x<3$: the extremes are $x$ and $6$, so $x+6=3+4$, $x=1$.
- $3\le x\le6$: $x+4=3+6$, $x=5$.
- $x>6$: $x+3=4+6$, $x=7$.

So the lengths are $\{1,3,4,6\}$, $\{3,4,5,6\}$ or $\{3,4,6,7\}$.

The plane bisects the volume iff it passes through the centre of the prism (the cut solids are congruent by the point reflection through the centre; if the plane misses the centre, one half strictly contains the reflected image of the other). The plane's point above the centre of the base rectangle has height equal to the average of the four $x_i$, which is $\frac{\min+\max}2$ (because of the parallelogram relation). The centre of the prism is at half the height $h$, so $h=\min+\max$:
- $\{1,3,4,6\}$: $h=7$,
- $\{3,4,5,6\}$: $h=9$,
- $\{3,4,6,7\}$: $h=10$.

The volume is $3\cdot7\cdot h=21h$, and the sum of all possible volumes is $21(7+9+10)=546$.

**Answer: 546**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-07.title: Linearity of expectation
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-07.body:
Whether or not a game is played is decided by earlier games, and each game that is played is won by its blue side with probability $\frac23$. So by linearity the expected number of blue-side wins is $\frac23\cdot E[\text{number of games played}]$.

Call the teams $A$ (blue in game 1) and $B$. Write series outcomes as strings of winners.
- Ends in 3 games: $AAA$ or $BBB$. $P(AAA)=\frac23\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac13=\frac2{27}$ (after each $A$ win, $B$ is blue), $P(BBB)=\frac13\cdot\frac13\cdot\frac13=\frac1{27}$. Total $\frac19$.
- Ends in 4 games: the strings $ABAA,AABA,ABBB$ (first game won by $A$) have probability $2\left(\frac23\right)^3\frac13+\left(\frac23\right)^2\left(\frac13\right)^2=\frac{20}{81}$, and $BABB,BBAB,BAAA$ have probability $2\left(\frac23\right)^2\left(\frac13\right)^2+\frac23\left(\frac13\right)^3=\frac{10}{81}$. Total $\frac{10}{27}$.

The 4th game is played with probability $1-\frac19=\frac89$ and the 5th with probability $1-\frac19-\frac{10}{27}=\frac{14}{27}$. Hence the expected number of games is $3+\frac89+\frac{14}{27}=\frac{119}{27}$, and the expected number of blue-side wins is $\frac23\cdot\frac{119}{27}=\frac{238}{81}$.

**Answer: $\frac{238}{81}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-07.title: Exact recursion check
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-07.body:
Let $E(a,b,\text{blue})$ be the expected number of future blue-side wins when $A$ has $a$ wins, $B$ has $b$ wins and the given team is blue. Evaluating this recursion from $(0,0,A)$ with blue win probability $\frac23$ (a short computation over the at most $19$ states) gives $\frac{238}{81}$, agreeing with the count above.

**Answer: $\frac{238}{81}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-08.title: Evaluate the polynomial at 0 and -1
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-08.body:
Let $P(x)=\left(x-\frac1{k-1}\right)\left(x-\frac1k\right)\left(x-\frac1{k+1}\right)-\frac1k=(x-\alpha_k)(x-\beta_k)(x-\gamma_k)$. Then
$$\alpha_k\beta_k\gamma_k=-P(0)=\frac1{(k-1)k(k+1)}+\frac1k=\frac{k}{k^2-1},$$
$$(1+\alpha_k)(1+\beta_k)(1+\gamma_k)=-P(-1)=\left(1+\tfrac1{k-1}\right)\left(1+\tfrac1k\right)\left(1+\tfrac1{k+1}\right)+\frac1k=\frac{k^2+3k-1}{k(k-1)}.$$
The general term is therefore
$$\frac{k}{k^2-1}\cdot\frac{k^2+3k-1}{k(k-1)}\cdot\frac1{k+1}=\frac{k^2+3k-1}{(k-1)^2(k+1)^2}.$$
Partial fractions give
$$\frac{k^2+3k-1}{(k-1)^2(k+1)^2}=\left(\frac{1/2}{k-1}-\frac{1/2}{k+1}\right)+\left(\frac{3/4}{(k-1)^2}-\frac{3/4}{(k+1)^2}\right).$$
Both parts telescope from $k=2$: the first sums to $\frac12\left(1+\frac12\right)=\frac34$, the second to $\frac34\left(1+\frac14\right)=\frac{15}{16}$. The total is $\frac34+\frac{15}{16}=\frac{27}{16}$.

**Answer: $\frac{27}{16}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-09.title: Reflect A over the midpoint of BC
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-09.body:
Let $A'$ be the reflection of $A$ across the midpoint of $BC$, so $ABA'C$ is a parallelogram. Since $AB\parallel CA'$ and $AC\parallel BA'$, we get $A'C\perp CY$ ($CY$ lies on $CH\perp AB$) and $A'B\perp BZ$. The condition $YC\cdot CA=ZB\cdot BA$ with $CA=A'B$, $BA=A'C$ gives $\frac{A'C}{CY}=\frac{A'B}{BZ}$, so the right triangles $A'CY$ and $A'BZ$ are similar. If the similarity preserved orientation then $A'Y\ge A'C$, $A'Z\ge A'B$ would force $YZ\ge BC$, contradicting $YZ<BC$; so it reverses orientation. By the converse of Jacobi's theorem for triangle $A'BC$ (cevians $BX$, $CX$ and $A'X$ concur with the perpendiculars to $BC$ at $B$, $C$ which meet at infinity), $X$ lies on the line through $A'$ perpendicular to $BC$.

Drop $D,D'$ as the feet of the perpendiculars from $A,A'$ to $BC$. Triangle $ABD$ is an $8$-$15$-$17$ triangle and $ADC$ is $15$-$20$-$25$, so $BD=8$, $AD=15$, $DC=20$, $D'C=8$ and $DD'=12$. The point $X$ is on line $A'D'$ at distance $2$ from $BC$; only the choice on the same side as $A$ (inside the triangle's strip) makes $YZ<BC$, so $X$ is $2$ above $D'$ and its height above $A$'s foot is $15-2=13$ (vertical difference).

Thus $AX=\sqrt{12^2+13^2}=\sqrt{313}$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{313}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-09.title: Coordinate check
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-09.body:
With $B=(0,0)$, $C=(28,0)$, $A=(8,15)$, $H=\left(8,\frac{32}3\right)$ and $X=(x,\pm2)$, solving $YC\cdot25=ZB\cdot17$ gives (besides solutions with $YZ>28$) exactly $X=(20,2)$, for which $YZ\approx19.5<28$. Then $AX^2=12^2+13^2=313$.

**Answer: $\sqrt{313}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-10.title: Cases for Brian's seat
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-10.body:
Let $n\ge2$ be the number of people. Label seats $0,\dots,n-1$ in passing order with Stephanie at $0$; Brian is at $\pm1$.

*Brian at $-1$:* $2024\equiv-1\pmod n$, so $n\mid2025$, and Stephanie gets the ball again after $k$ more passes iff $n\mid k+2024$. Such $n\ge2$ exists iff $\gcd(k+2024,2025)=\gcd(k-1,2025)>1$ (take $n$ equal to this gcd).

*Brian at $+1$:* $2024\equiv1\pmod n$, so $n\mid2023$, and we need $n\mid k+2024$; possible iff $\gcd(k+2024,2023)=\gcd(k+1,2023)>1$.

So $k$ works iff $\gcd(k-1,2025)>1$ or $\gcd(k+1,2023)>1$. With $2025=3^2 5^2$ and $2023=7\cdot17^2$, count the complement: $1\le k\le2024$ with $3\nmid k-1$, $5\nmid k-1$, $7\nmid k+1$, $17\nmid k+1$. Shifting $k\to k-1$, this is the number of $0\le j\le2023$ with $3\nmid j$, $5\nmid j$, $7\nmid j+2$, $17\nmid j+2$.

By the Chinese remainder theorem each block of $3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot17=1785$ consecutive $j$ contains $2\cdot4\cdot6\cdot16=768$ such values. The remaining $239$ values $j\in[1785,2023]$ behave like $j\in[0,238]$ (period $1785$): in $[0,209]$ there are $2\varphi(105)=96$ values with $3,5,7$ conditions, of which $5$ ($j=32,83,134,151,202$) fail the $17$ condition, leaving $91$; in $[210,238]$ there are $15$ values with $3\nmid j,5\nmid j$, of which $3$ ($j=219,229,236$) fail the other conditions, leaving $12$.

The complement has $768+91+12=871$ elements, so the answer is $2024-871=1153$.

**Answer: 1153**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-10.title: Computer check
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-10.body:
Directly testing every $k$ from $1$ to $2024$ for the existence of a table size $n$ satisfying $n\mid 2024\mp1$ and $n\mid k+2024$ gives $1153$ good values.

**Answer: 1153**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-11.title: Area of the triangle from PA, PB, PC
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-11.body:
Take $ABC$ with side $1$ and centroid $G$. Rotate $P$ by $60^\circ$ about each of $A,B,C$ to get $P_A,P_B,P_C$. The triangles $PP_AB$, $P_BCP$, $AP P_C$... each have sides $PA,PB,PC$, so they are congruent to the triangle $\Delta$ with those side lengths; the triangles $PAP_A$, $PBP_B$, $PCP_C$ are equilateral with sides $PA,PB,PC$. The hexagon $AP_ABP_BCP_C$ has area $2[ABC]$ and decomposes into these six triangles, so
$$3[\Delta]=2[ABC]-\frac{\sqrt3}4\left(PA^2+PB^2+PC^2\right)\ ,\quad [\Delta]=\frac13\left(\frac{\sqrt3}2-\frac{\sqrt3}4(PA^2+PB^2+PC^2)\right).$$
By Leibniz's relation $PA^2+PB^2+PC^2=GA^2+GB^2+GC^2+3GP^2=1+3GP^2$. Therefore $[\Delta]=\frac{\sqrt3}{12}-\frac{\sqrt3}4GP^2$.

This is at least $\frac29[ABC]=\frac{\sqrt3}{18}$ iff $GP^2\le\frac19$, i.e. $GP\le\frac13$ (and then $[\Delta]>0$, so non-degenerate).

The region is the disk of radius $\frac13$ about $G$ intersected with the triangle. The inradius is $\frac{\sqrt3}6<\frac13$, so the disk sticks out across each side in a circular segment of half-angle $\arccos\frac{\sqrt3/6}{1/3}=30^\circ$. Its area is $\pi\cdot\frac19-3\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac19\left(\frac\pi3-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)=\frac\pi{18}+\frac{\sqrt3}{12}$. Dividing by $[ABC]=\frac{\sqrt3}4$:
$$\frac{\pi}{18}\cdot\frac4{\sqrt3}+\frac13=\frac{2\pi\sqrt3}{27}+\frac13=\frac{9+2\pi\sqrt3}{27}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{9+2\pi\sqrt3}{27}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-12.title: Beatty sequences
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-12.body:
Let $r=3-\sqrt3$ and $s=3+\sqrt3$; then $\frac1r+\frac1s=1$, so the Beatty sequences $\lfloor kr\rfloor$ and $\lfloor ks\rfloor$ partition the positive integers. Also $r-1=2-\sqrt3$ and $\lfloor(k+1)(r-1)\rfloor=\lfloor(k+1)r\rfloor-(k+1)$ increases by $1$ from $k$ to $k+1$ exactly when $\lfloor(k+1)r\rfloor-\lfloor kr\rfloor=2$.

An induction over the successive $k$ with $\lfloor(k+1)r\rfloor-\lfloor kr\rfloor=2$ (using that $\lfloor jr\rfloor$ and $\lfloor js\rfloor$ never coincide) shows that for such $k$, $\lfloor\lfloor(k+1)(r-1)\rfloor\cdot s\rfloor=\lfloor kr\rfloor+1$, while for the other $k$ it equals the value at the previous such $k$. So the subtracted term is determined by the position of $\lfloor kr\rfloor$ relative to the elements $\lfloor js\rfloor$.

The integers $1,\dots,132$ are split by the multiples $\lfloor js\rfloor$ ($j\le28$) into $28$ classes, each containing $3$ or $4$ elements of the $r$-sequence; counting ($104$ elements of the $r$-sequence in $[1,132]$) gives $8$ classes with $3$ elements and $20$ with $4$. A 3-element class contributes squares $1^2,2^2,1^2$, a 4-element class $1^2,2^2,3^2,1^2$. Hence the sum over $k=1,\dots,104$ is $6\cdot8+15\cdot20=348$. The term $k=104$ contributes $1$ and the term $k=0$ contributes $0$, so the requested sum over $0\le k\le103$ is $348-1=347$.

**Answer: 347**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-12.title: Direct computation
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-12.body:
Computing each term with exact arithmetic (high-precision $\sqrt3$) for $k=0,1,\dots,103$ and adding the squares gives $347$.

**Answer: 347**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-13.title: Cyclic shifts
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-13.body:
Cyclic shifts of a solution are solutions, so $\mathbb Z/46$ acts on the solution set and $N\equiv$ (number of solutions with fewer than $46$ distinct shifts) $\pmod{46}$, counted appropriately: a tuple with period $d\mid46$ has $d$ distinct shifts and its orbit has size $d$; orbits of size $46$ contribute multiples of $46$.

Periods $d\in\{1,2,23,46\}$. If $d=1$ or $d=23$ then $x_i=x_{i+23}$ for all $i$ and the sum of $35$th powers is even, impossible since $253$ is odd (and $2024$ is even). If $d=2$, then the tuple is $(a,b,a,b,\dots)$ and $23(a^{35}+b^{35})\equiv253\pmod{2024}$. Dividing by $23$ ($2024=23\cdot88$, $253=23\cdot11$) this is $a^{35}+b^{35}\equiv11\pmod{88}$ with $1\le a,b\le88$. Then $N\equiv$ the number of such pairs $(a,b)$ modulo $46$.

By CRT split into mod $8$ and mod $11$ (the number of $(a,b)$ with residues in each system multiplies):
- Mod $8$: $a^{35}+b^{35}\equiv3$. Odd residues satisfy $n^{35}\equiv n\pmod 8$ (as $n^2\equiv1$), and $n^{35}$ for even $n$ is $0$ mod $8$. So one of $a,b$ is even and the other is $\equiv3$: $4\cdot2=8$ pairs.
- Mod $11$: $a^{35}+b^{35}\equiv0$. Here $n^{35}\equiv n^5\equiv\pm1$ for $n\not\equiv0$ ($n^{10}\equiv1$), with $5$ residues each. Either both $a,b\equiv0$ ($1$ pair) or one has $n^5\equiv1$, the other $-1$ ($2\cdot5\cdot5=50$ pairs): total $51$.

So the number of pairs is $8\cdot51=408\equiv40\pmod{46}$.

**Answer: 40**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-13.title: Computer check
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-13.body:
Computing the exact number of $46$-tuples by convolving the distribution of $x^{35}\bmod2024$ $46$ times (exact integers) and reducing the coefficient of $253$ modulo $46$ gives $40$.

**Answer: 40**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-14.title: Angle chase, then similar triangles
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-14.body:
Let $H$ be the orthocenter. Since $AKBI$ is cyclic, $\angle BAK=\angle BIK$; expressing both angles through $B$ and $C$ by angle chasing in the orthic configuration (the official solution does this via $\angle CBE-\angle FEB=\angle DAC-\angle BAH$) gives $2B-C=90^\circ$, so $B=45^\circ+\frac C2$.

The condition $\angle IWF=\angle FWE$ means $W$ lies on the circle $(EBI)$: indeed $\angle BIE=\angle BAH=\angle FEB=\angle IEB$ (by the cyclic condition), so for $W'$ the second intersection of $(EBI)$ with line $BF$, $\angle IW'F=\angle FW'E$; and $W$ is the unique such point of the ray (second intersection with the Apollonius circle), so $W=W'$ and $WIBE$ is cyclic.

Then $\angle WBI=\angle WEI$ gives $\triangle WIB\sim\triangle WFE$, so
$$\frac{WB}{WI}=\frac{WE}{WF}=\frac{IB}{IF}=\frac{\sin C}{\sin B}.$$
With $\cos C=\frac25$: $\sin C=\frac{\sqrt{21}}5$, and $\sin B=\sin(45^\circ+\frac C2)=\frac{\sqrt2}2\left(\cos\frac C2+\sin\frac C2\right)$ with $\cos\frac C2=\sqrt{\frac{1+\cos C}2}=\sqrt{\frac7{10}}$ and $\sin\frac C2=\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos C}2}=\sqrt{\frac3{10}}$. So $\sin B=\frac12\left(\sqrt{\frac75}+\sqrt{\frac35}\right)$ and
$$\frac{WB}{WI}=\frac{2\sqrt{21}/5}{\sqrt{7/5}+\sqrt{3/5}}=\frac{2\sqrt{21}}{\sqrt{35}+\sqrt{15}}=\frac{2\sqrt{21}(\sqrt{35}-\sqrt{15})}{20}=\frac{7\sqrt{15}-3\sqrt{35}}{10}.$$

**Answer: $\frac{7\sqrt{15}-3\sqrt{35}}{10}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-14.title: Numerical check
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-14.body:
Constructing the triangle with $C=\arccos\frac25$ and $B=45^\circ+\frac C2$, computing $K,I$ (and verifying $A,K,B,I$ concyclic), and then locating $W$ on ray $BF$ by solving $\angle IWF=\angle FWE$ numerically gives $WB/WI\approx0.93626$, which equals $\frac{7\sqrt{15}-3\sqrt{35}}{10}$.

**Answer: $\frac{7\sqrt{15}-3\sqrt{35}}{10}$**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-15.title: Bijection with permutations
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-15.body:
Consider the analogous functions $f:[n]\to[n]$ with $k$ ranging over $1\le k\le n-1$. There is a bijection between roughly monotonic functions and permutations $\sigma$ of $[n]$: given $\sigma$, put $f(\sigma^{-1}(1))=n$, and then process $j=2,\dots,n$ in turn, setting $f(\sigma^{-1}(j))=f(\sigma^{-1}(j-1))$ if $j-1$ comes before $j$ in $\sigma$, and $f(\sigma^{-1}(j))=f(\sigma^{-1}(j-1))-1$ otherwise. The inverse repeatedly picks the leftmost position where $f$ attains its maximum among the unassigned positions. (Checking that both maps land in the right sets and are mutually inverse is a direct induction.)

The codomain $\{2,\dots,6\}$ in the problem corresponds to $f:[7]\to[7]$ whose range has size at most $5$ (shifting values), i.e. permutations of $[7]$ that split into at most $5$ increasing runs of consecutive integers $j,j+1,\dots$ in the sense above. The bad permutations use $6$ or $7$ such blocks. With $7$ blocks (all singletons) there is $1$ permutation. With $6$ blocks exactly one block has length $2$, namely $\{i,i+1\}$ for $i=1,\dots,6$ with $i$ before $i+1$ and the rest in decreasing order of values; counting positions gives $6,20,34$ for $i=1,2,3$ and, by symmetry, $34,20,6$ for $i=4,5,6$ (sum $120$).

The number of roughly monotonic functions is therefore $7!-1-120=4919$.

**Answer: 4919**

chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-15.title: Brute force
chmmc-cmm-2024-individual-15.body:
A direct enumeration of all $5^7=78125$ functions $f:\{1,\dots,7\}\to\{2,\dots,6\}$, testing the condition for each $k$, finds exactly $4919$ roughly monotonic functions.

**Answer: 4919**
